transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-06-25
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Aisha (Solutions), Rahul (CTO, SummitLink), Mei (Infra Lead), Tom (Product), Sara (Security)

Summary: Intro / partner orientation for SummitLink to evaluate Redwood Private + Dedicated options; focus on hybrid SaaS integration for inference routing, VPC connectivity, benchmark plans, and security/compliance needs.

00:00 Lena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — if you can say name and role — and then we will get into a short orientation of how we typically work with partners on hybrid GPU + SaaS integrations.
00:08 Rahul (SummitLink): Rahul, CTO. Excited to dig in.
00:10 Mei (SummitLink): Mei here, infra.
00:12 Tom (SummitLink): Tom, product.
00:13 Sara (SummitLink): Sara, security.
00:15 Marcus (Redwood): Hi all, Marcus SE — I'll go through serving/runtime and the benchmark approach.
00:18 Aisha (Redwood): Aisha — solutions, will follow up on pilots and integration ops.
00:22 Lena (Redwood): Cool. Super high level: SummitLink's ask was to understand options for on-prem or VPC-hosted inference for your SaaS product, routing between your control plane and our Redwood Private, and what a pilot looks like especially on throughput and cost. Is that still right?
00:30 Rahul (SummitLink): Yes, that's it. We have a hybrid topology. Some customer data stays in SummitLink VPCs — cannot leave region. We also want Redwood to handle burst capacity for peak times.
00:38 Lena (Redwood): Great. Two things we usually propose: Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable steady-state throughput, plus Private (VPC) connectors for data residency. We can also route overflow to hosted variants if needed with fallbacks.
00:50 Tom (SummitLink): Fallbacks — how seamless are they? We can't have a change in response format for customers.
00:55 Marcus (Redwood): We do model-variant compatibility mapping. So the API response schema is preserved via the same interface; when we route to a quantized variant or hosted fallback, we apply post-processing and model mapping to keep outputs consistent. There can be slight latency differences, but payload structure stays fixed.
01:10 Mei (SummitLink): What about KV cache and prefix caching? Most of our inference is chat-like with long context.
01:16 Marcus (Redwood): We support KV caching and prefix cache at the router layer. A few caveats: cross-region cache warmup costs, and for private deployments we can configure local cache (keeps latency low). Note — sometimes our transcriber shows "KV cash" in docs, sorry transcription slur — it's KV cache.
01:30 Rahul (SummitLink): Got it. Also interested in batching. Peak concurrency hits a few hundred reqs/sec; we need tail latency under 300ms for single-turn answers. Can you meet that?
01:40 Marcus (Redwood): For single-turn sub-300ms at that concurrency you typically need a mix of smaller batch sizes + optimized kernels — depends on model size. For 7B-class models on A100 or equivalent with our kernel selection and continuous batching we can hit ~200-250ms p50 for 1k tokens; but p99 might be higher. We recommend a short benchmark to validate your token length distribution.
02:00 Tom (SummitLink): You mentioned kernel selection — any concerns about customer-managed hardware? We're planning to test with on-prem Ampere 80GB.
02:06 Marcus (Redwood): We maintain a model profile catalog that maps to hardware — Ampere 80GB is a common target. For on-prem we ship a private runtime that does the kernel selection locally; some proprietary optimizations need driver-level support. We'll provide a checklist of driver/kernel versions.
02:20 Sara (SummitLink): From security: SOC 2 + ISO are table stakes. Also want audit logs, KMS integration, and the ability to rotate keys using our HSM.
02:28 Aisha (Redwood): We have SOC2 and ISO documents; Private deployments integrate with customer KMS (KMIP/HSM or cloud KMS). Audit logs are configurable and can push to your logging stack via secure syslog or S3 with encryption. We'll include the packet.
02:40 Mei (SummitLink): Network wise, we prefer VPC peering over public endpoints. Any special requirements?
02:45 Marcus (Redwood): VPC peering or private link is a common pattern. We'll need CIDR ranges, allowed ports, and throughput expectations. For high throughput we recommend dedicated ENIs and jumbo frames. Also keep an eye on NAT gateway egress if you have egress-limited subnets.
02:59 Rahul (SummitLink): What about data retention — we must not persist PII beyond session. Can you disable logging of user inputs in private mode?
03:05 Aisha (Redwood): Yes — Private mode can be configured to disable or truncate logs at the token level; you can also route logs to your S3 with lifecycle rules. We can ship a configuration that redacts PII on ingest, but you'll want to include sample prompts and examples for our eval team.
03:20 Tom (SummitLink): Are there customers doing a similar hybrid? Curious about references.
03:24 Lena (Redwood): We have a few enterprise customers who run hybrid: private VPC ingress plus burst to hosted; we can share anonymized patterns and a case study. I'll attach the deck.
03:33 Mei (SummitLink): On licensing, how does pricing differ for Dedicated vs Private? We want committed cost predictability.
03:38 Lena (Redwood): Dedicated is commit-based monthly/annual capacity — lower unit costs, SLA-backed latency; Private has a platform fee + support and sometimes a lower per-token charge depending on commit. For hybrid pilots we'll propose an MLP (minimum viable pilot) pricing model so you can run realistic loads without full commitment.
03:55 Rahul (SummitLink): Competitor question: we talked to CloudX — they push fully managed only, not private. Any migration risks?
04:02 Marcus (Redwood): Migration risk is mostly around model artifacts and KV cache. We provide exportable artifacts and a compatibility layer. Unlike fully managed vendors, our Private option gives you control over keys and logs.
04:15 Sara (SummitLink): Any SOC2/penetration testing schedule? We will need to align our internal auditors.
04:22 Aisha (Redwood): We run annual penetration tests and can share the last red-team summary. For pilots we can offer on-demand scans and provide jump boxes for your security team to validate. We'll coordinate with Sara — please send the contact list.
04:35 Marcus (Redwood): Quick note on quantization: you mentioned cost sensitivity. Our Optimize toolkit suggests per-workload quant profiles — e.g., 4-bit quant for embedding-heavy workloads; mixed-precision for chat workloads. We will propose quantization recommendations after the pilot corpus analysis.
04:52 Tom (SummitLink): For the benchmark run, what telemetry do you collect? We can't share user text.
04:58 Marcus (Redwood): We can run synthetic traces derived from token distributions and mock user dialogs you provide. Telemetry includes latency histograms, token counts, memory usage, and KV cache hit/miss rates. We can keep the payload sanitized.
05:15 Lena (Redwood): Okay let's recap next steps and owners. We'll: 1) send pilot scope + pricing (Lena), 2) attach SOC2/ISO packet and network diagram template (Aisha), 3) Marcus will produce a benchmark runbook and sample tests, 4) SummitLink to confirm network/CIDR and security contacts.
05:36 Rahul (SummitLink): That works. Also we may want a short demo of your Console observability and routing policies.
05:42 Lena (Redwood): We'll schedule a Console demo during the benchmark week — Marcus and Aisha will present.
05:48 Sara (SummitLink): One more — can you sign an NDA before we share any internal prompts?
05:52 Lena (Redwood): Yes, we'll route an NDA via legal.
05:55 Marcus (Redwood): Great thanks everyone.
06:00 Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription: minor mis-hearings present (KV cash), some speaker overlap; timestamps approximate.
